title: Student Conduct, Discipline, and Restorative Practices

content.title: No physical punishment - an absolute rule
content.text:
Corporal punishment is prohibited in all Eduversal Partner Schools. There are no exceptions, and the ban covers every setting, including boarding houses and religious instruction. It includes hitting or striking with a hand or an object, pushing, and forcing a student to do physical exercise as a penalty. It also includes painful or humiliating stress positions, and withholding food, drink, sleep or access to a toilet. It includes any punishment that causes physical pain, fear or public humiliation.

No cultural, religious or disciplinary reason makes it acceptable. A staff member who uses physical punishment faces disciplinary action under the staff code of conduct. The matter is reported to the DSL (Designated Safeguarding Lead) and handled under Section 9. Under UU No. 35/2014, physical violence against a child is prohibited. Physical violence is also the first of the six forms of kekerasan named in Permendikdasmen No. 6/2026 (BSAN).

Staff may use reasonable physical intervention only to prevent immediate harm to a person. Every such intervention is recorded and reported to the Principal the same day.

Discipline at Eduversal Partner Schools has an educational purpose. It is not simply about punishment. The final goal of education is self-governance. Students learn not only to understand right from wrong but also to use that understanding to make ethical choices.

Everyone who takes part in the school community is subject to its rules and regulations. Joining this community brings a duty to follow its standards. When students make mistakes, discipline aims to guide them back to understanding what is appropriate. It also helps them act on that understanding.

The school has wide freedom (discretion) to develop its discipline criteria and policy. This depends on each student accepting the duty to follow the lawful rules of the school community. This policy helps school officials protect the educational environment. They do this by setting clear expectations for behavior and clear consequences. When necessary, they also remove distractions from that environment.
content.title: 22.1.1 Educational Purpose of Discipline

content.text:
These principles guide all discipline decisions and interventions:

**Restorative Focus:** The school gives priority to repairing harm, restoring relationships and bringing students back into the community. These come before punishment alone. Consequences are necessary, but the main aim is to help students learn from mistakes and build stronger character.

**Due Process:** Every student has the right to be heard and to understand what they are accused of. Every student also has the right to give their side before any consequence is decided. No student shall be punished without a chance to respond to the concerns. This principle follows Indonesian child protection requirements for the fair treatment of minors.

**Proportionality:** Consequences must match how serious the behavior is. Each decision considers the context, the student's intent and history, and their stage of development. It also considers any circumstances that make the behavior less serious (mitigating) or more serious (aggravating). A first-time minor offense should not receive the same consequence as a repeated serious violation.

**Consistency:** Behavior expectations and consequences apply fairly and equally to all students. This is true whatever their academic standing, family background, financial status or social connections. The school must avoid any appearance of favoritism or discrimination in discipline matters.

**Cultural Sensitivity:** The school respects different cultural backgrounds. It also keeps universal standards of respect and safety. In Islamic boarding schools, discipline includes Islamic values and character development principles. In all schools, EAL (English as an Additional Language) learners get suitable support to understand expectations. Cultural differences in communication styles are considered during investigations.

**Student Voice:** Students help develop classroom expectations. They help resolve conflicts through peer mediation and restorative conversations. Student input is valued when policy is developed and reviewed.

**Positive Reinforcement:** The school recognizes and celebrates positive behavior, as well as dealing with misconduct. A whole-school approach to behavior management includes consequences for inappropriate behavior. It also includes recognition of excellent conduct.

**Transparency:** All rules, expectations and consequences are clearly explained to students and parents. They are given in clear, simple language (English and Bahasa Indonesia). There should be no surprises about expected behavior or about the consequences that may follow a violation.
content.title: 22.1.2 Core Principles

content.text: The discipline framework helps students develop the Schoolwide Learner Outcomes (SLOs), especially:
content.title: 22.1.3 Alignment with School Values and Learning Outcomes

items: Ethical Leadership: Students show integrity, take responsibility for their actions, and model positive behavior for peers.
Global Competence: Students show respect for different views and settle conflicts through discussion and understanding.
Communication: Students raise concerns in the right way and take a helpful part in resolving conflicts.
Wellbeing: Students learn to manage their own behavior (self-regulation) and help create a positive school climate.

content.text: The framework also includes the Profil Pelajar Pancasila (P5) character competencies:

items: Beriman, Bertakwa kepada Tuhan YME, dan Berakhlak Mulia: Acting with moral integrity guided by faith and ethical principles.
Gotong Royong: Working together to keep a positive community and helping peers make good choices.
Mandiri: Taking personal responsibility for their own behavior and self-control.
Bernalar Kritis: Thinking about actions and their consequences; making careful decisions.
Berkebinekaan Global: Respecting diversity and treating all community members with dignity.

content.text: Cross-Reference: See Section 1.2 for the network vision, mission and core values. See Section 2.4 for the requirements on including Profil Pelajar Pancasila.

Student conduct and discipline connect with safeguarding in several important ways. Peer-on-peer harm is harm between students, such as bullying, harassment or abuse. It is dealt with through both the behavior policy and safeguarding procedures. When a discipline matter involves a possible safeguarding concern, the Designated Safeguarding Lead (DSL) must be informed. The DSL may take the lead in managing the situation. Discipline responses must never put child protection at risk. The safety and wellbeing of all students comes first.

Cross-Reference: See Section 9 for the full safeguarding policies and reporting procedures.
content.title: 22.1.4 Relationship to Safeguarding

content.text: The Student Code of Conduct applies to all students in Eduversal Partner Schools, from Early Years to A-Level. The Code covers behavior in these situations:
content.title: 22.2.1 Scope and Application

items: During school hours on school premises
Before and after school while on campus
During school-sponsored activities, whether on or off campus
On school transport (buses and vehicles arranged by the school)
During school trips, excursions, and residential programs
At school-related events (sports competitions, performances, ceremonies)
In any situation where behavior affects the school community or damages the school's reputation
Online and on social media, when this is related to the school or affects members of the school community
For boarding students, in dormitories and residential facilities at all times

content.title: 22.2.2 Behavioral Expectations Matrix
content.text: The table below shows expected behaviors by domain. It is aligned with the SLOs and P5 competencies:

content.title: Domain: Respect for Self
content.text:
**Expected Behaviors:** Keep personal dignity and a positive self-image. Take pride in appearance and presentation. Show integrity and honesty in all academic work and interactions. Make healthy choices. Develop self-discipline and self-regulation skills.

**Practical Examples:** Wearing the proper uniform correctly; keeping good personal hygiene; completing your own work without cheating. Being on time; taking care of personal belongings; making positive choices about health and safety.

content.title: Domain: Respect for Others
content.text:
**Expected Behaviors:** Treat all community members (students, teachers, staff, visitors) with kindness and courtesy. Listen actively. Value different views and backgrounds. Use appropriate language. Keep appropriate physical boundaries. Support and encourage peers.

**Practical Examples:** Using polite words (please, thank you, excuse me); not interrupting when others speak; including classmates in activities. Avoiding gossip and rumors; respecting personal space; offering help to people in need; celebrating others' successes.

content.title: Domain: Respect for Learning
content.text:
**Expected Behaviors:** Come to class prepared, with the required materials. Take an active part in lessons. Complete assignments carefully and on time. Support the learning of others. Keep disruptions to a minimum. Use feedback in a positive way. Show intellectual honesty.

**Practical Examples:** Bringing textbooks, notebooks and supplies; joining in class discussions; asking questions when confused. Meeting deadlines; keeping noise at a suitable level; not distracting classmates; citing sources properly.

content.title: Domain: Respect for Environment
content.text:
**Expected Behaviors:** Care for school property and facilities. Keep classrooms, common areas and grounds clean. Act responsibly toward the environment. Use resources appropriately. Report damage or repairs that are needed.

**Practical Examples:** Disposing of waste properly (recycling where available); keeping desks and lockers tidy; not writing on walls or furniture. Turning off lights and fans when leaving rooms; treating books and equipment carefully; reporting broken items.

content.title: Domain: Safety and Security
content.text:
**Expected Behaviors:** Follow all safety rules and procedures. Report safety concerns promptly. Make safe choices in physical activities. Look out for the welfare of peers. Cooperate during safety drills. Avoid bringing dangerous items to school.

**Practical Examples:** Following laboratory safety rules; taking part seriously in fire and earthquake drills; reporting hazards to teachers. Using playground equipment safely; not playing dangerous games or challenges; keeping emergency exits clear.

content.title: Domain: Digital Citizenship
content.text:
**Expected Behaviors:** Use technology responsibly and ethically. Follow the Acceptable Use Policy. Behave appropriately online. Protect personal privacy and the privacy of others. Report cyberbullying or inappropriate content. Use AI tools only as permitted.

**Practical Examples:** Not sharing passwords; avoiding inappropriate websites; being respectful in online communication. Not posting embarrassing photos of others; reporting online concerns to adults; acknowledging AI help when it is used.

Core values stay the same, but behavior expectations match each stage of development:

**Early Years and Primary (K-6):** The focus is on basic social skills, following instructions and kindness to others. Children also learn to take care of belongings and to follow classroom routines. Expectations are simple, concrete and reinforced often. Adults take the main responsibility for teaching and modeling expected behaviors.

**Lower Secondary (Years 7-8):** Expectations for self-management, organization and taking responsibility increase. Students begin to develop conflict resolution skills. They begin to understand the consequences of their choices. Peer relationships become more important, so social dynamics need attention.

**Upper Secondary IGCSE (Years 9-10):** Students are expected to show more independence, leadership and accountability. Expectations for academic integrity increase. Students should model positive behavior for younger students and contribute to school culture.

**A-Level (Years 11-12):** Expectations for self-regulation, integrity and leadership are close to adult level. Students act as role models and may take formal leadership positions. This stage prepares them for the independence and responsibility expected at university.
content.title: 22.2.3 Age-Appropriate Expectations

content.text:
Schools use several channels to make sure everyone in the community understands behavior expectations:

**Student and Parent Handbook:** The full Code of Conduct is published in the Student and Parent Handbook, in both English and Bahasa Indonesia. Printed copies are given out at enrollment. Digital versions are on the school website and the EduNav parent portal.

**Enrollment Agreement:** Parents and students sign an acknowledgment. In it, they confirm that they have received and read the Code of Conduct. They also agree to follow it as a condition of enrollment.

**Orientation Programs:** Special sessions during new student orientation explain expectations, consequences and support systems. Assemblies at the start of the year remind returning students of the expectations.

**Classroom Agreements:** In the first week of school, teachers and students develop class expectations together. These agreements follow school-wide standards and also address each classroom's own situation. Classroom agreements are displayed clearly and referred to regularly.

**Visual Reminders:** Posters, displays and signs suited to students' ages reinforce key expectations around the school. Common areas show school values and behavior expectations in student-friendly language.

**Regular Reinforcement:** Teachers build behavior expectations into daily routines. They recognize positive behavior and deal with concerns promptly. Assemblies cover behavior themes from time to time.

**Parent Communication:** Regular newsletters, parent meetings and parent-teacher conferences include discussion of behavior expectations and student conduct. Parents receive annual reminders about the Code of Conduct.
content.title: 22.2.4 Communication of Expectations

subsections.title: Classification of Behaviors and Progressive Consequences

content.text: Behaviors are sorted into four levels. The level depends on how serious the behavior is, its impact on others and its potential for harm. This step-by-step system helps make sure responses are proportionate. It also gives clear routes for escalation. Classification considers:
content.title: 22.3.1 Behavior Classification Framework

items: What the behavior was and how serious it was
The effect on individuals and on the community
Intent (deliberate vs. accidental)
How often it happens (a first offense or a repeated pattern)
Context and circumstances
Student's age and developmental level
Any special educational needs or other circumstances that matter here

content.text: Definition: Behaviors that disrupt teaching and learning or class order, but do not cause significant harm to other people or property. The teacher or staff member who sees the behavior usually deals with it immediately. If the same offense happens three times, it moves up to Level 2. Examples of Level 1 Behaviors:
content.title: 22.3.2 Level 1: Minor Infractions (Classroom-Managed)

items: Arriving late to class (up to 10 minutes)
Not bringing required learning materials
Small uniform problems (shirt not tucked in, no tie)
Not working on the task; too much chatting during lessons
Incomplete or late homework
Eating or drinking in class without permission
Minor disruptions (tapping, humming, minor horseplay)
Sleeping in class
Failure to follow classroom procedures
Not participating in compulsory activities
Disposing of trash improperly
Using electronic devices without permission (first offense)

content.text: Possible Responses to Level 1:

items: Verbal reminder or redirection
A signal without words (moving closer, eye contact, a gesture)
Private conversation with student
Seat change
Brief written reflection
Losing a small privilege (e.g., choosing an activity)
Break-time task or brief duty
The teacher contacts the parent (if a pattern appears)
Recording in teacher notes

content.text: Handling Authority: The classroom teacher, or the staff member who saw the behavior. Documentation: Teachers keep their own records. A formal incident report is not required unless a pattern appears (3+ occurrences). Timeline: Dealt with immediately, during or after class.

Definition: Actions that disrupt the learning environment more widely, repeat Level 1 behaviors, or show disrespect, but do not endanger others' safety. These require action by the School Culture (SC) Coordinator. They usually involve communication with the homeroom teacher and the parents. Examples of Level 2 Behaviors:
content.title: 22.3.3 Level 2: Moderate Infractions (School Culture Coordinator-Managed)

items: Repeated Level 1 offenses (3+ occurrences)
Several different Level 1 offenses in a short period
Not completing Level 1 consequences
Using a mobile phone in class without permission, again and again (a first offense is a Level 1 matter under 22.3.2)
Missing class without permission (truancy)
Leaving school grounds without authorization
Disrespectful language or attitude toward staff
Inappropriate language (profanity, vulgar speech)
Minor vandalism (graffiti, small damage to property)
Rough play that could lead to injury
Academic dishonesty (first offense, minor)
Not following exam rules (minor cases)
Spreading rumors or gossip that causes distress
Opening or viewing inappropriate content on school devices
Breaking the dormitory curfew or schedule (boarding schools)

content.text: Possible Responses to Level 2:

items: Meeting with SC Coordinator
Confiscation: the school takes away property (devices, inappropriate items)
After-school detention (30-60 minutes)
Saturday detention for boarding schools
Written parent notification
Parent conference (phone or in-person)
Behavior contract with specific targets
Restorative conversation with affected parties
Community service within school
Losing privileges for a time (taking part in extracurricular activities, special events)
Cannot leave campus early (boarding schools)
Written reflection and apology
All Level 1 responses may also apply

content.text: Handling Authority: The SC Coordinator, who consults the Homeroom Teacher. Documentation: A formal Incident Report is filed in EduNav, with a copy to the homeroom teacher. The parent notification is recorded. Timeline: Investigation and response within 48 hours.

Definition: Actions against people or property that cause or could cause harm, repeated Level 2 behaviors, or serious breaks of school values. These require formal disciplinary procedures, written warning letters, and mandatory parent involvement. These behaviors are serious. But they may still be handled without long-term exclusion if suitable interventions are put in place. Examples of Level 3 Behaviors:
content.title: 22.3.4 Level 3: Serious Infractions (Principal-Managed)

items: Repeated Level 2 offenses
Accumulated multiple Level 2 offenses
Physical fighting without serious injury
Bullying or harassment (verbal, social, physical)
Intimidation or threats toward others
Theft or extortion (forcing someone to hand over money or items) of small value
Significant damage to property (on purpose or reckless)
Repeated academic dishonesty
Forging (faking) documents, signatures, or records
Having inappropriate materials (pornography, etc.)
Gambling on school premises
Defying authority (refusing a direct instruction from staff)
Leaving campus without permission during school hours
Inappropriate physical contact, or crossing personal boundaries
Recording others without consent
Severe cyberbullying or online harassment (less severe cyberbullying is a Level 2 matter; every report is recorded)
Behavior in public that damages the school's reputation

Behavior in a relationship that breaks school expectations is handled pastorally (with care and guidance). The school counselor handles it at Level 1 or 2 (for applicable schools). Any relationship that involves coercion (pressure or force), a power imbalance, or a safeguarding concern is NEVER treated as student misconduct. It is referred to the DSL (Designated Safeguarding Lead) under Section 9

content.text: Possible Responses to Level 3:

items: First or Second Warning Letter
In-school suspension (1-3 days)
Out-of-school suspension (1-3 days)
Mandatory parent conference with Principal
Restorative conference with victim(s)
Formal apology (written and/or verbal)
Restitution for damages or theft
Behavioral intervention plan
Mandatory counseling sessions
Removal from leadership positions
Suspension from extracurricular activities
Report to Cambridge (for exam-related misconduct)
Cannot go home on weekends (boarding schools, for a limited time)
All Level 1-2 responses may also apply

content.text: Handling Authority: The Principal, with input and recommendations from the SC Coordinator. Documentation: A formal investigation report, and a Warning Letter that the parents acknowledge. All records are kept in EduNav and in the student file. Timeline: The investigation is completed within 5 school days. The decision is communicated in writing.

Definition: Behaviors that endanger others' safety, involve illegal activities, cause serious harm, or deeply violate the school's values. These may result in long-term suspension or expulsion, and law enforcement (the police) could become involved. Level 4 behaviors are often also safeguarding concerns that require DSL involvement. Examples of Level 4 Behaviors:
content.title: 22.3.5 Level 4: Severe Infractions (Discipline Committee/Board-Managed)

items: Level 3 offenses repeated even after interventions
Having, using, or distributing (giving or selling) illegal drugs or alcohol
Having weapons or dangerous items
Serious physical assault causing injury
Severe bullying or harassment
Sexual harassment or assault
Threats of serious violence
Arson or fire-setting
Major theft or extortion
Serious vandalism causing significant damage
Criminal activity on or off campus
Bringing drugs, alcohol, or weapons to school
Distributing illegal substances
Gang-related activity
Serious violations of Indonesian law
Actions that put the safety of the school community at risk
Examination malpractice (serious cases, such as stealing papers)
Actions that seriously damage the school's reputation

content.text: Possible Responses to Level 4:

items: Third Warning Letter
Long-term suspension (4-10 days or more)
Expulsion recommendation to Yayasan Board
Police notification and involvement
Report to relevant authorities
Mandatory external counseling or intervention
Informing the DSL and following safeguarding procedures (if applicable)
Report to Cambridge Assessment (for exam malpractice)
Withdrawal of Cambridge examination candidacy
All Level 1-3 responses may also apply

content.text: Handling Authority: Discipline Committee (makes the recommendation); Yayasan Board (makes the expulsion decision). Documentation: A full investigation file; Discipline Committee minutes; the Yayasan Board decision record; a record of all communications. Timeline: Emergency response as needed. Formal investigation within 5 school days. Discipline Committee within 5 extra days. Yayasan Board decision within 10 school days of the Committee recommendation.

Warning letters are formal records of serious misconduct. The School Culture Coordinator prepares them, and they are issued with the Principal's approval. They act as an official record and as the route for escalation (moving to more serious steps):

**First Warning Letter (Surat Peringatan Pertama/SP-1):** Issued for Level 3 violations. The letter records the incident and names the policies that were broken. It sets out the behavior changes expected and states the consequences of further violations. Parents must confirm in writing that they received it. The letter stays in the student file for the academic year.

**Second Warning Letter (Surat Peringatan Kedua/SP-2):** Issued for further Level 3 violations, or for continued patterns of concern after SP-1. It includes a behavior contract with specific, measurable targets and a timeline. A mandatory parent conference with the Principal is required. The student may be placed on behavioral probation with defined conditions.

**Third Warning Letter (Surat Peringatan Ketiga/SP-3):** Issued for Level 4 violations, or for continued serious misconduct after SP-2. It starts the process of considering expulsion. The student may be suspended immediately until the Discipline Committee reviews the case. Parents are formally told that expulsion is possible.

**Important Notes on Warning Letters:**
content.title: 22.3.6 Warning Letter System

items: For severe Level 4 violations, warning letters may be skipped. The case then goes directly to suspension or expulsion consideration.
Second and third warning letters may be issued for repeated Level 3 violations, without necessarily following the order. This means a build-up of serious incidents may justify SP-2 or SP-3 directly.
Warning letters from earlier academic years may be taken into account in decisions. But they do not carry forward automatically.
Warning letters are confidential documents. They are shared only with relevant school staff and the student's family.

content.text: When decision-makers choose the right classification (level) and consequence, they consider: Mitigating Factors (may make the response less severe):
content.title: 22.3.7 Factors Affecting Classification and Consequences

items: A first offense, with no earlier discipline record
Genuine remorse (real regret) and accepting responsibility
Full cooperation with investigation
Voluntary disclosure before discovery
Circumstances suggesting provocation
Significant personal stressors or challenges
Developmental or special educational needs that affect judgment
Cultural misunderstanding (especially for new students or EAL (English as an Additional Language) learners)
Peer pressure, with evidence that the student took part unwillingly

content.text: Aggravating Factors (may make the response more severe):

items: Premeditation or planning
Leadership role in group misconduct
Targeting vulnerable individuals
Repeat offense despite prior intervention
No remorse (regret), or not accepting responsibility
Trying to hide evidence or mislead investigators
Involving others, or encouraging them to take part
Breaking trust while holding a position of trust (student leader, etc.)
Significant harm caused to victim(s)
Actions during examinations or official events

content.text: All disciplinary procedures follow these principles:
content.title: 22.4.1 General Principles of Procedure

items: Presumption of Innocence: Students are treated as innocent until the evidence supports a finding that they are responsible.
Right to Be Heard: Students get the chance to give their side of the story before consequences are decided.
Confidentiality: Discipline matters are handled confidentially. Information is shared only with those who need to know.
Timeliness: Investigations and decisions are finished as quickly as possible. This keeps worry and disruption low.
Documentation: All significant actions are recorded in writing and kept securely.
Support: Students get suitable support during the whole process, including access to counseling if needed.

content.text: Step 1: Initial Report. The teacher or staff member who sees or learns of an incident reports it to the SC Coordinator. They use the standard Incident Report Form. For minor incidents (Level 1), teachers may deal with it directly and record it in their own notes. For Level 2 and above, a formal report should be submitted within 24 hours of the incident or its discovery. The initial report includes:
content.title: 22.4.2 Investigation Process

items: Date, time, and location of incident
Description of what happened (facts, not interpretation)
Names of students involved
Names of witnesses
Any immediate actions taken
Any physical evidence available

content.text: Step 2: Initial Assessment. The SC Coordinator reviews the report and makes an initial assessment to decide:

items: Preliminary classification level
Urgency of response required
Whether safeguarding procedures need to be started
Whether the student(s) should be kept out of classes during the investigation
Who needs to be told (Principal, DSL, parents)

content.text: Step 3: Evidence Collection. The SC Coordinator (or the Principal for Level 3-4) collects evidence:

items: Written statements from all witnesses (students and staff)
A review of relevant records (attendance records, earlier incidents, etc.)
Collecting physical evidence (if applicable)
Checking CCTV footage, if it is relevant and available
Screenshots of digital communications, if cyberbullying is involved
Any other relevant information

content.text: Witness statements should be taken one by one, so that witnesses do not work together on their accounts. For younger students, statements may be spoken, with an adult writing down the information. Step 4: Student Interview. The student who is said to have committed the offense is interviewed:

items: The interview takes place in a private, calm setting
The student is told what the allegations are and is given a chance to respond
The student may have a support person present (homeroom teacher, counselor)
For serious matters (Level 3-4) or younger students, parents may be present
The student's account is recorded in writing
The student is asked to name any witnesses or give any evidence that supports them

content.text: Step 5: Parent Notification. Parents are told about the investigation:

items: For Level 1: The teacher decides, usually if a pattern appears
For Level 2: A phone call, then written communication (email/letter)
For Level 3-4: An immediate phone call, formal written notice, and an invitation to a meeting

content.text: Parent notification includes:

items: What concern is being investigated
Process being followed
Opportunity for parent input
Information about the support available to the student
Timeline for decision

content.text: Step 6: Analysis and Recommendation. The investigator (SC Coordinator or Principal) studies all the evidence:

items: Judges how believable and reliable the information is
Considers context and circumstances
Weighs mitigating and aggravating factors
Reviews student's prior record
Considers whether the outcome is consistent with how similar cases have been handled
Prepares written summary of findings
Recommends a classification (level) and a consequence

content.text: Step 7: Decision and Communication. The person or body with the right authority makes the decision:

items: Level 1: Teacher (immediate, may be verbal)
Level 2: SC Coordinator (within 48 hours, in writing to parents)
Level 3: Principal (within 5 days, formal letter to parents)
Level 4: Discipline Committee/Board (within 10 days of Committee meeting)

content.text: The decision communication includes:

items: Summary of incident and findings
Classification level determined
Consequence(s) imposed
Rationale for decision
Any conditions or requirements
Support offered to student
Information about appeal rights (for Level 3-4)
Level 1: Dealt with immediately or on the same day
Level 2: Investigation and response within 48 hours
Level 3: Investigation completed within 5 school days; the decision is communicated on the same day the investigation is completed

Level 4: Emergency measures within 24 hours; full investigation within 5 school days; Discipline Committee within 5 extra days; Yayasan Board (for expulsion) within 10 school days of Committee recommendation
content.title: 22.4.4 Timeline Standards

content.text: In complex cases, timelines may be extended. Parents are notified when this happens.
Misconduct during Cambridge examinations follows extra procedures: During Examination:
content.title: 22.4.5 Special Procedures for Examination Misconduct

items: The invigilator (exam supervisor) records the concern on an Incident Report
The student is allowed to continue the exam (unless they are actively disrupting others)
The invigilator tells the Examinations Officer immediately after the exam
The student is not told about the concern during the exam (so that worry does not affect their performance)

content.text: Post-Examination:

items: The Examinations Officer investigates and prepares a report
The student is interviewed and given a chance to respond
The Principal reviews the case and decides if malpractice happened
If malpractice is found, a report goes to Cambridge on Form 4 within the required time limit
Cambridge makes the final decision on the consequences for the examination

content.text: Cross-Reference: See Section 10.5 for the full Cambridge malpractice procedures and reporting requirements.
When a situation needs immediate action (danger to oneself or to others, criminal activity, etc.):
content.title: 22.4.6 Emergency Procedures

steps: Make sure everyone involved is safe immediately
Separate student(s) from situation
Contact emergency services if needed (police, medical)
Tell the Principal immediately (or the most senior staff member available)
Contact parents as soon as possible
Document all actions taken
Activate safeguarding procedures if applicable
Provide support to affected parties
Preserve evidence for investigation
The Principal may suspend the student immediately while the investigation takes place

content.title: External escalation under Permendikdasmen No. 6/2026 (BSAN)
items: The internal ladder in this section (SC Coordinator, Principal, Discipline Committee, Yayasan Board) is for ordinary conduct matters only.

If an incident involves kekerasan in any of its six BSAN forms (fisik, psikis, seksual, digital, sosial, or spiritual), the matter leaves the conduct ladder. The Principal is then the single accountable officer.
The school handles non-criminal cases itself, "secara edukatif, proporsional dan berkeadilan" (in an educative, proportionate and fair way). The DSL is involved.

Serious cases go outside the school to the Pokja BSAN at kabupaten/kota level. There they receive verification, an initial analysis and referral. At the same time, criminal matters go to the police (Unit PPA).
Note on timeframes: BSAN sets no legal deadline for reporting. The 48-hour and 5-school-day timelines in this section are Eduversal network standards. They are not legal requirements.

content.title: Decision authority by infraction level
rows: GM / Foundation Representative (for suspension over 3 days), Parents
Discipline Committee; Yayasan Board for expulsion
Eduversal, and also the authorities if the matter is criminal or involves kekerasan under BSAN

content.text: Definition: The student serves the suspension at school, in a supervised space away from regular classes. The student keeps doing schoolwork and reflects on their behavior through guided activities. Duration: 1-3 days. Authorization: Principal. Procedures:
content.title: 22.5.1 In-School Suspension

steps: The Principal gives parents a written notice with the dates and the reason
The student goes to the assigned supervision area (not the regular classroom)
Teachers give the student work to complete
The student completes the reflection activities set by the SC Coordinator or Counselor
The student may eat lunch apart from other students
A reintegration (return) meeting takes place before the student goes back to regular classes
Boarding students serve the suspension in an assigned area, supervised by a tutor

content.text: Student Responsibilities During In-School Suspension:

items: Arrive on time and stay in the assigned area
Complete all assigned academic work
Complete reflection activities
Behave respectfully toward supervising staff
Not communicate with other students during the suspension

content.text: Definition: The student is removed from school for a set period. The student may not take part in any school activities during the suspension. Duration: 1-10 days, depending on how serious the case is. Authorization:
content.title: 22.5.2 Out-of-School Suspension

items: 1-3 days: Principal
4+ days: the Principal, and the GM/Foundation Representative is informed

content.text: Procedures:

steps: The Principal gives parents a written notice with the dates, the reason and the conditions for return
Parents must collect the student from school (the student is not sent home alone)
The student may not come onto school grounds during the suspension
The student may not attend school events or activities during the suspension
Teachers give the student work to complete at home
A return-to-school conference with the parent, student, Principal and SC Coordinator is required
Reintegration plan developed and documented
Follow-up monitoring schedule established

content.text: For Boarding Students:

items: The student goes home for the whole suspension
If going home is not possible, another supervised arrangement is made
Parents are responsible for supervising the student during the suspension

content.text: Definition: Expulsion means a student is removed from the school permanently. It is the most serious consequence. It is kept for the most serious violations, or for cases where other interventions have failed. Authorization: Yayasan Board (final decision), based on the Discipline Committee's recommendation. Expulsion Criteria: Expulsion may be considered when:
content.title: 22.5.3 Expulsion Process

items: The student has committed an extremely serious Level 4 violation
The student has received three warning letters and has not improved
The student's continued presence is an unacceptable risk to others
The student has committed criminal acts that affect the school community
All reasonable interventions have been tried, and none has worked
The behavior is deeply incompatible with membership of the school

content.text: Formal Process: Step 1: Principal Recommendation. The Principal writes a full recommendation to the Discipline Committee. It includes:

items: Full records of the incident(s) that led to the recommendation
Student's disciplinary history
Interventions attempted and outcomes
Evidence supporting recommendation
The effect on the victim(s) and the school community
Any mitigating factors considered

content.text: Step 2: Discipline Committee Review. The Discipline Committee meets within 5 school days of receiving the recommendation. Committee members:

items: Principal (Chair)
GM/Foundation Representative
School Counselor
Teacher Representative (not directly involved in incident)
SC Coordinator (presenting officer, non-voting)

content.text: The Committee reviews all the records and may ask for more information. Step 3: Hearing. The student and parents are invited to come before the Committee:

items: Written notice is given at least 3 school days before the hearing
The notice includes the specific allegations, a summary of the evidence and the possible outcome
The family may send a written statement in advance
At the hearing, the family can present their view and any supporting evidence
The family may ask questions about the evidence
Committee members may ask the family questions
The family may bring an advocate (but not as formal legal representation)

content.text: Step 4: Committee Deliberation. After the hearing, the Committee discusses the case in private:

items: Considers all evidence and testimony
Determines whether expulsion is warranted
If the outcome is not expulsion, decides on a different consequence
Writes a recommendation to the Yayasan Board (for expulsion) or a written decision (for a different consequence)

content.text: Step 5: Yayasan Board Decision (for expulsion). When the Committee recommends expulsion, the Yayasan Board:

items: Reviews the Committee's recommendation and the supporting records
May ask the family to appear or to send an extra statement
Makes the final decision within 10 school days of the Committee's recommendation
The decision needs a majority vote of the Board members present
The decision is final (but it can be appealed, as set out in Section 22.6)

content.text: Step 6: Communication. The family receives a written decision. It includes:

items: Decision reached (expulsion or alternative)
Effective date
Rationale for decision
Practical information (collecting belongings, records transfer, etc.)
Appeal rights and process

content.text: Immediate Actions Following Expulsion Decision:

items: The student's access to school systems is ended
The student collects personal belongings (with supervision, at an agreed time)
Academic records are prepared for transfer to the new school
Refunds are calculated according to school policy
Cambridge is informed if the student was registered for examinations
A confidential summary is prepared for any school that asks for one

content.text: Students expelled from Eduversal Partner Schools are generally not eligible for readmission. Exceptional cases are different, for example when a long time has passed or there is clear evidence of rehabilitation. In such cases, a family may ask for the case to be reconsidered:
content.title: 22.5.4 Readmission After Expulsion

items: The petition is sent in writing to the GM/Foundation Representative
Must be at least one full academic year after expulsion
Includes evidence of changed circumstances/behavior
The Yayasan Board decides whether to consider the petition
If the petition is considered, the full re-application process is required
No guarantee of acceptance

content.text: Students and parents have the right to appeal disciplinary decisions on Level 3 and Level 4 consequences. An appeal must be based on one or more of these grounds:
content.title: 22.6.1 Right to Appeal

items: Procedural Error: The investigation or decision process did not follow the set procedures, and this affected the outcome.
New Evidence: Important new evidence has come to light. It was not available during the original investigation and could change the decision in an important way.
Disproportionate Consequence: The consequence does not fit the offense, considering all the circumstances and how similar cases have been handled.
Misinterpretation of Facts: The evidence does not support the findings of fact, or there was a serious error in understanding what happened.

content.text: Appeals may not be based just on disagreeing with the decision or on hoping for a lighter outcome.
Step 1: Written Appeal Submission
content.title: 22.6.2 Appeal Procedures

items: Send a written appeal to the GM/Foundation Representative
Deadline: Within 5 school days of receiving the disciplinary decision
Include: the specific grounds for appeal, supporting evidence or argument, and the outcome you are asking for
Receipt of the appeal is confirmed within 2 school days

content.text: Step 2: Review of Appeal. Recusal is mandatory. Anyone involved in the original decision, including on the Discipline Committee, cannot hear the appeal. That person must delegate it to a senior colleague who was not involved. The GM/Foundation Representative:

items: Reviews original investigation documentation
Reviews appeal submission
May ask either party for more information
May interview the people involved if necessary
Does not investigate again. Instead, checks whether the process was fair and the decision reasonable

content.text: Step 3: Appeal Decision. A written response is given within 10 school days of the appeal being submitted:

items: Appeal upheld (the original decision is cancelled or changed)
Appeal partially upheld (consequence modified)
Appeal denied (original decision stands)
Includes rationale for decision

content.text: Step 4: Final Appeal (Expulsion Cases Only). For expulsion decisions, families may send a final appeal to Eduversal Central Management:

items: Deadline: Within 10 school days of GM appeal decision
Submitted in writing to Eduversal Central Office
Central Management checks for significant concerns about the procedure
A decision is given within 15 school days
This decision is final
For suspension: The suspension generally continues during the appeal, unless the urgency of the appeal review justifies delaying the suspension
For expulsion: The student usually stays suspended (does not attend school) during the appeal process
If the appeal succeeds: The suspension days may be removed from the record. In expulsion cases, the student is reinstated.
content.title: 22.6.3 Effect of Appeal on Consequences

content.text: Restorative practices bring a change in thinking. We stop asking: What rule was broken and what punishment is deserved? Instead, we ask: Who was harmed, what are their needs, and how can we make things right? This approach recognizes that misconduct harms relationships and the community. True accountability involves repairing that harm. Restorative practices at Eduversal Partner Schools:
content.title: 22.7.1 Philosophy of Restorative Practice

items: Build positive relationships proactively
Respond to conflict and wrongdoing by dealing with the harm
Involve everyone affected in finding solutions
Focus on the future (making things right) rather than only the past (assigning blame)
Develop students' social-emotional skills and sense of responsibility
Build stronger community bonds instead of just punishing individuals

content.text: Restorative practices add to traditional discipline. They do not replace it. For serious offenses, restorative processes may be used together with formal consequences. They deal with the harm to relationships while clear boundaries stay in place.

These practices build good relationships and prevent conflict:

**Community Circles (Circles for Community Building):** Regular class meetings (weekly in Primary, biweekly in Secondary). Students sit in a circle and take turns to share, using a talking piece. Circles build relationships and give students a voice. They develop communication skills and create shared agreements. Topics might include weekends, class challenges, celebrating achievements, or exploring values.

**Affective Statements:** Teachers use "I-statements" to say how the impact of a behavior makes them feel. They avoid language that accuses. For example, a teacher says: "I feel concerned when assignments aren't submitted because I want to make sure you're learning". The teacher does not say: "You're lazy and irresponsible." This shows students how to understand and talk about feelings (emotional literacy). It invites dialogue rather than defensiveness.

**Restorative Questions:** Simple questions used in everyday situations to help students think about impact:
content.title: Tier 1: Universal/Preventive Practices (All Students, All Settings)

items: What happened?
What were you thinking at the time?
Who has been affected by what happened?
How have they been affected?
What do you think you need to do to make things right?
content.title: 22.7.2 Continuum of Restorative Approaches

content.text:
Fair Process: Involving students in decisions that affect them (classroom rules, seating, activity choices), so they feel ownership and commitment. Explaining the reasons for rules and decisions.

Tier 2: Responsive Practices (Targeted Intervention for Minor-Moderate Conflicts). These practices respond to conflicts and harm:

Restorative Conversations: A conversation between the person who caused harm and the person harmed. It is one-on-one or in a small group, and a trained staff member leads it. Used for minor conflicts, misunderstandings and repairing relationships. Duration: 15-30 minutes. Structure:

steps: Each person shares their view (using a talking piece)
The facilitator helps identify the harm caused
The person who caused harm acknowledges the impact
Discussion of how to make things right
Agreement reached and follow-up planned

content.text: Peer Mediation: Trained student mediators help other students solve conflicts through a structured conversation. It is suitable for disputes between students when both sides are willing to take part. School staff train and supervise the student mediators. Peer Mediation Process:

steps: Mediators explain the ground rules (respect, honesty, confidentiality)
Each party shares their view without being interrupted
The two parties find what they agree on and where they differ
Brainstorm solutions together
Reach agreement and document
Follow-up scheduled

content.text:
Small Group Conferences: A meeting, led by a facilitator, with the student who caused harm, the people affected and relevant supporters (teachers, parents). Used for more serious incidents that affect several people. Duration: 45-60 minutes.

Tier 3: Intensive Practices (Serious Incidents Requiring Formal Process)

Formal Restorative Conferences: A structured conference for serious incidents, involving:

items: Student who caused harm and their parent(s)
Victim(s) and their parent(s) (if willing to participate)
Affected community members (teachers, other students who saw what happened, etc.)
Trained facilitator (Counselor or external specialist)
Principal or SC Coordinator as observer

content.text: Conference Process:

steps: The facilitator explains the process and the ground rules (90-120 minutes)
The person who caused harm describes what happened and what they were thinking
Each affected person describes how it affected them
Parents/supporters share their perspectives
The person who caused harm responds to what they have heard
The group discusses what needs to happen to make things right
A written agreement is made, with specific commitments
Follow-up plan established

content.text: Taking part is voluntary for victims. They may take part in person, send a written statement, ask a representative to speak for them, or not take part. The conference can still go ahead without the victim. It then focuses on the responsible student's accountability. Reintegration Circles: These support a student's return to class or school after a suspension or a long absence because of a discipline matter. The circle welcomes the student back. It gives the student a chance to share their commitments. It also lets the community say what it needs from the student from now on.

Agreements made through restorative processes may include:

**Acknowledgment:** A written or spoken statement of what happened, accepting responsibility. This is not about shame. It is about honest accountability.

**Apology:** A sincere apology to the people harmed. It may be spoken, written, or both. A good apology names the specific harm, shows real regret, promises change, and asks what else is needed.

**Restitution:** Practical repair for material harm—paying for damaged items, replacing stolen property, or repairing the damage caused. Restitution may be financial or through service.

**Service Contribution:** Community service that helps the people harmed or the wider community. It should be meaningful and, where possible, connected to the harm (e.g., helping to look after areas that were vandalized).

**Behavioral Commitments:** Specific, measurable promises about future behavior. They should be realistic and achievable.

**Support Needed:** The support the student needs to succeed (counseling, academic help, check-ins with a mentor, etc.).

**Follow-up Plan:** A timeline for checking that the agreement is completed, who will monitor it, and what happens if the agreement is not fulfilled.

All agreements are written down, signed by the participants, and filed in EduNav. Completion of each agreement is tracked and reported.
content.title: 22.7.3 Restorative Agreement Components

content.text: Staff receive training to use restorative approaches:
content.title: 22.7.4 Training for Restorative Practice

items: All Teachers: a 6-hour introduction on professional development days. It focuses on affective statements, restorative questions, and classroom circles
Homeroom Teachers: an extra 3-hour training on leading community circles and restorative conversations
SC Coordinator and Counselor: 2-day intensive training on leading formal restorative conferences, plus refresher training every year
Student Peer Mediators: an 8-hour training program on mediation skills, confidentiality, and when to refer, with ongoing supervision

content.text: Cross-Reference: See Section 12.6 for overall professional development framework and DTP requirements.

Definition and Scope: Eduversal Partner Schools strictly prohibit bullying in all forms. Bullying means repeated, intentional behavior that causes physical, emotional, or psychological harm. It usually involves a real or perceived imbalance of power between the bully and the target. A single severe incident may also count as bullying. Bullying is prohibited:
content.title: 22.8.1 Anti-Bullying Policy

items: On school premises
During school-related activities
On school transportation
Online, when it affects members of the school community (cyberbullying)
Off-campus when it affects the school environment or community

content.text:
Types of Bullying: Physical Bullying: Hitting, kicking, pushing, tripping, spitting, damaging property, unwanted physical contact, threatening gestures, or blocking someone's way.

Verbal Bullying: Name-calling, insults, teasing, threats, intimidation, offensive comments about appearance/ability/background, spreading rumors.

Social/Relational Bullying: Leaving someone out on purpose, manipulating friendships, public humiliation, spreading rumors, damaging someone's reputation, isolating individuals.

Cyberbullying: Harassment through technology. This includes offensive messages, sharing embarrassing images/videos without consent, and pretending to be someone else online. It also includes excluding someone from online groups, sharing private information, creating fake accounts, and online threats.

Response: Bullying is treated as at least a Level 3 infraction. There is one exception: lower-severity cyberbullying is a Moderate (Level 2) incident under the Digital Citizenship & AI Framework §8.2. Every bullying or cyberbullying report is recorded, and severity decides the response. Severe or repeated bullying may count as Level 4. The response includes:

items: Immediate intervention to stop the bullying
Support for the target (counseling, safety planning, monitoring)
Investigation following Level 3-4 procedures
A consequence for the bully that matches how severe the bullying was
A restorative conference, if the target is willing
Follow-up monitoring to make sure the bullying does not continue

Involving the parents of both students, based on safeguarding judgment. Where a family member may be involved, or contact could increase risk, parents are not contacted automatically before the risk is assessed

content.text: Prevention: Schools run anti-bullying programs, including:

items: Teaching about bullying in assemblies and in the PSHE (Personal, Social, Health and Economic education) curriculum
Ways for students to raise and report concerns (student voice)
Training for staff on recognizing and responding to bullying
Clear communication that bullying is unacceptable
Positive bystander training for students
Monitoring high-risk places and times
Regular school climate surveys to measure how common bullying is

content.text: Reporting: Students can report bullying through:

items: Telling any trusted adult (teacher, counselor, staff)
Anonymous reporting through a suggestion box or an online form
Speaking to SC Coordinator or Principal directly
Parents contacting the school for their child

content.text:
All reports are taken seriously and investigated. Students will not face any negative consequences for reporting in good faith.

Cross-Reference: See Section 9.13 for bullying within the safeguarding framework (Specific Safeguarding Contexts). See Section 21.4 for cyberbullying in the digital environment.

**Statement:** Academic integrity is central to the educational mission of Eduversal Partner Schools. Students should do their own work honestly, credit their sources properly, and act with integrity in all assessments. Academic dishonesty damages learning and breaks Cambridge examination regulations.

**Prohibited Behaviors:**

**Plagiarism:** Presenting other people's work, ideas, or words as their own without proper credit. This includes copying from sources (including the internet) without citation, and submitting bought or downloaded work. It also includes paraphrasing too closely without credit.

**Collusion:** Working together without permission on work that is meant to be done individually. Collaboration is encouraged when it is permitted. But submitting joint work as individual work is collusion.

**Cheating:** Using unauthorized materials or help during assessments. This includes notes, electronic devices, communication with others, copying another student's work, and getting advance information about assessment content.

**Fabrication:** Inventing or falsifying data, sources, citations, or experimental results. This includes citing sources the student did not actually use and inventing quotations.

**Facilitating Dishonesty:** Helping others to be academically dishonest—sharing work for copying, giving unauthorized help during assessments, or letting others copy.

**AI Misuse:** Using artificial intelligence tools to produce work without permission or acknowledgment. When AI use is permitted, students must disclose that they used it and the kind of help they received.

**Teaching Academic Integrity:** Schools actively teach academic integrity:
content.title: 22.8.2 Academic Integrity Policy

items: Age-appropriate teaching on citation and referencing
A clear explanation of what counts as dishonesty
Practice with paraphrasing and summarizing
Discussion of why integrity matters
Guidance on appropriate use of AI tools
Academic integrity agreement signed by students

content.text:
Consequences: First Offense (Minor): Level 2 response—a teaching conversation about integrity, a chance to be re-assessed, and parent notification. The focus is on teaching, not punishment.

Repeated Offenses or Serious First Offense: Level 3 response—warning letter, zero on the assignment with no redo, possible course grade penalty, academic integrity contract.

Examination Misconduct: It is reported to Cambridge Assessment International Education, in line with Centre requirements. Cambridge decides the consequences. These may include disqualification from the subject or from all subjects.

For Cambridge Examinations: Any suspected malpractice during Cambridge examinations must be:

items: Recorded on an incident report during or after the exam
Reported to the Principal and the Examinations Officer immediately
Investigated promptly
Reported to Cambridge using Form 4 if malpractice is suspected
Subject to Cambridge's decision on the consequences

content.text: Cross-Reference: See Section 6.12 for academic integrity in the assessment policy. See Section 10.5 for Cambridge malpractice reporting procedures.

Acceptable Use: Students must follow the Acceptable Use Policy (AUP) for all school technology and personal devices used for school purposes. Students and parents sign the AUP at enrollment and every year after that.

Mobile Phone Policy: Mobile phones bring both opportunities and risks in schools. Schools use the following framework: General Rules:
content.title: 22.8.3 Technology and Digital Citizenship Policy

items: Mobile phones must be collected by homeroom teachers at the start of the school day (day schools) or by dormitory tutors (boarding schools)
Phones are stored securely and returned at the end of the day or at set times
Unauthorized use during school hours is prohibited
The school may inspect the contents of a device if there is reasonable suspicion of a policy violation

content.text: Boarding School Schedule (Example):

items: Saturday: 05:00-22:00
Other times: Permission is required, with a recommendation from a teacher/tutor

content.text: Consequences for Unauthorized Use:

items: First offense: The device is held until the end of the school day (this is a Level 1 matter under 22.3.2)
Second offense: The device is held until a parent or guardian collects it

Third offense: The device is held until a parent or guardian collects it in person, and there is a meeting to agree a plan. The school never permanently keeps, sells, or gets rid of a student's property

content.text:
Parents may collect a confiscated device during the confiscation period with a signed letter from the parents. If there is a specific concern about content on a personal device, the school does not force a student to unlock it. The device is kept secure and a parent or guardian is contacted. Any examination of the device takes place with the parent present and with the safeguards in 22.8.4 applied. If a criminal offense is suspected, the matter is referred to the police and is not investigated by the school.

AI Tools: Artificial intelligence tools may only be used within teacher-approved guidelines. Unauthorized or undisclosed AI use in assessments is academic dishonesty. When AI use is permitted, students must:

items: Only use approved AI tools
Disclose AI assistance in their work
Keep their own original thinking and personal voice
Not submit AI-generated content as their own work

content.text: Online Conduct: Students must behave respectfully and appropriately in all school-related online interactions:

items: No cyberbullying, harassment, or threats
No sharing inappropriate content
Respect other people's privacy (no sharing photos without consent)
Represent school appropriately on social media
Report concerns about online safety

content.text: Cross-Reference: See Section 21 for the full Digital Learning and Technology policy, including the full AUP.

Authority: The school may carry out searches to keep students safe. School-owned storage (lockers, desks, and school-issued equipment) stays school property and may be checked routinely. A student's person, pockets, bag, or dormitory room is never searched routinely. Any search of these always follows the individual-search safeguards below. Types of Searches: Routine/Random Searches:
content.title: 22.8.4 Search and Seizure Policy

items: Routine checks cover school-owned storage only (lockers and school-issued equipment) and are announced in advance
Supervised by Principal and/or Head of Boarding
The search team includes the SC Coordinator, the academic coordinator, dormitory staff, and picket teachers (teachers on duty)
All lockers and school-issued equipment in the selected area are checked equally
Items checked: lockers, desks, and school-issued devices and equipment (school-owned storage only — never a student's person, pockets, bag, or dormitory room)
Focus: electronic devices, prohibited items

content.text: Individual Searches:

items: Cover any search of a student's person, pockets, bag, or dormitory room
Require reasonable suspicion of policy violation
Authorized by Principal
Carried out by a staff member of the same gender, with a witness present
The student is told the reason for the search
The parent is told afterward (unless this would put the investigation at risk)

content.text: Search Procedure:

steps: The routine-check schedule is published to students and parents in advance. A search of a person, a bag, or a dormitory bedroom requires reasonable suspicion, the student's presence, and Principal authorization. Each such search is logged for DSL review
The search team brings label paper, collection bags, and documentation forms
Students are asked to stand away from their belongings
Belongings searched systematically
Items found are labeled to show who owns them, and recorded
Items are taken to the office for inspection
Owners of confiscated items are told, and consequences are applied according to policy

content.text: Prohibited Items: Items that may not be brought to school include:

items: Weapons (knives, sharp objects, items that could cause harm)
Drugs, alcohol, tobacco, vaping devices
Pornographic or inappropriate materials
Gambling equipment
Non-prescribed medicines (the clinic must hold them)
Items violating dress code
Unauthorized electronics during restricted times

content.text: Handling of Items:

items: Dangerous or illegal items: reported to the authorities and not returned
Prohibited but not illegal items: confiscated under the relevant policy. They may be returned to parents
Items held as evidence: kept until the investigation is complete
All confiscations documented

content.text: Prohibition: This rule covers alcohol, illegal drugs, tobacco, vaping products, and non-prescribed controlled substances. Having, using, supplying (selling or giving), or being under the influence of any of them is strictly prohibited. This applies on school premises, at school events and on school transportation. For boarding students, it also applies in dormitories. Response: Substance abuse violations are usually Level 4 infractions:
content.title: 22.8.5 Substance Abuse Policy

items: Immediate removal from class/activity
Parent notification
Possible police involvement for illegal substances
Mandatory counseling/intervention program
Suspension (length depends on circumstances)
Distribution: likely expulsion
First-time possession or use: serious consequences. These may not be expulsion if the student takes part in the intervention

content.text: Support: Students who come forward themselves about substance concerns before any incident may receive support instead of punishment:

items: Counseling and intervention services
Referral to appropriate professionals
Confidentiality maintained to extent possible
Monitoring and check-ins

content.text: The school aims to balance community safety with support for students who struggle with substance problems.

content.text: In Islamic Boarding Schools (Pesantren) and other residential programs, the Code of Conduct applies 24/7 for as long as the student lives there. Boarding students represent the school at all times.
content.title: 22.9.1 Extended Scope of Conduct Expectations

content.text: Extra expectations for boarding students include: Daily Schedule Compliance:
content.title: 22.9.2 Dormitory-Specific Expectations

items: Keeping to prayer times (fajr, dhuhr, asr, maghrib, isha for Islamic boarding)
Participation in mandatory study periods
Keeping lights-out and wake-up times
Coming to meals at the set times
Taking part in dormitory activities and programs

content.text: Room and Living Standards:

items: Keeping personal space and shared areas clean
Respecting roommates' belongings and space
Following room inspection standards
Proper care of school-provided furnishings
Not bringing prohibited items into dormitory

content.text: Gender Interaction:

items: Strict adherence to gender-appropriate areas
Following guidelines for interaction between genders
Not entering the dormitory areas of the opposite gender
Appropriate conduct in co-educational spaces

content.text: Leave and Movement:

items: Proper authorization to leave campus (written permission from parents kept on file)
Sign-out/sign-in procedures for all departures
Reporting whereabouts at all times
Not leaving the dormitory after curfew without a tutor's permission
Weekend home leave following the approved schedule

content.text: Self-Study Period Rules:

items: Staying in the set study areas during self-study time
Not using online shopping or non-educational websites
No eating in study rooms (heavy meals)
No music through speakers during study time
Not leaving the study room without a tutor's permission
Digital devices for learning only

content.text: Electronic Devices:

items: Dormitory tutors collect mobile phones and keep them safe
Use only during set times (usually weekends)
A recommendation letter is required for use outside scheduled times
The school may check device contents only when there is reasonable suspicion of a policy violation (see 22.8.3 and 22.8.4)
Progressive confiscation policy for violations

content.text: Handling Authority:
content.title: 22.9.3 Dormitory Discipline Protocols

items: Minor issues (Level 1): the Dormitory Tutor deals with them directly
Moderate issues (Level 2): the Dormitory Director works with the SC (School Culture) Coordinator
Serious issues (Level 3-4): the Principal handles them, with dormitory leaders involved

content.text: Dormitory-Specific Consequences: As well as the standard consequences, boarding students may face:

items: Extra cleaning or dormitory duties
Loss of weekend home leave privileges
Restriction to dormitory during free time
Earlier curfew or extended study hours
Loss of electronic device privileges
Temporary room reassignment
Loss of boarding privileges (for severe or repeated violations) before expulsion

content.text: Weekend Leave Restrictions:

items: Level 2 offenses: May lose one weekend leave
Level 3 offenses: May lose multiple weekend leaves
Repeated violations: a longer restriction on home leave

content.text: Communication with Home:

items: Parents are told about all significant behavior concerns
Regular update calls or messages from dormitory staff
Parent conferences may take place by video call if meeting in person is not possible

content.text: Staff spend longer with boarding students. This allows strong positive reinforcement (rewarding good behavior):
content.title: 22.9.4 Positive Recognition for Boarding Students

items: Recognition points for positive behavior (being on time, helping others, academic effort)
Points add up toward privileges or awards
Weekly/monthly recognition for exemplary students
Leadership opportunities for students whose conduct is consistently positive
Telling parents about positive progress

content.text: All behavior incidents and interventions must be recorded in EduNav. This keeps tracking consistent, shows patterns, and guides improvement: Incident Reports:
content.title: 22.10.1 Documentation Requirements

items: Full description of the incident (who, what, when, where)
Names of witnesses
Evidence collected
Initial response taken
Classification level assigned
Follow-up actions planned

content.text: Conference Notes:

items: Date, attendees, purpose of meeting
Key points discussed
Agreements reached
Action items and responsibilities
Follow-up scheduled

content.text: Warning Letters:

items: Formal letter with a summary of the incident and the expectations
Parent acknowledgment signature
Filed in student confidential file
Copy in EduNav

content.text: Intervention Records:

items: Behavioral intervention plans
Progress monitoring data
Support provided (counseling, mentoring, etc.)
Modifications made

content.text: Restorative Conference Records:

items: Participants and roles
Summary of conference process
Agreement reached (specific commitments)
Follow-up plan
Completion tracking

content.text: Monthly Analysis: The SC Coordinator reviews behavior data every month to find:
content.title: 22.10.2 Data Analysis and Reporting

items: Incident frequency and trends
Patterns by time, place and student group
Effectiveness of interventions
Students needing extra support
Environmental factors to address
Staff development needs

content.text:
A report goes to the Principal with recommendations.

Term Reports: Behavior data is included in school improvement reporting:

items: Total incidents by level
Disaggregation by grade, gender, type
Comparison to previous terms/years
Suspension and expulsion data
Restorative conference completion rates
Progress on behavioral KPIs

content.text:
Shared with the GM/Foundation Representative and included in the School Improvement Plan review.

Annual Review: a full analysis that guides policy updates:

items: Analysis of the full year's data and trends
Stakeholder feedback (staff, students, parents)
Effectiveness of current approaches
Recommendations for policy modifications
Professional development priorities for coming year
Resource needs identified

content.text:
Schools track these KPIs (key performance indicators) for student conduct:

Incident Rate:
content.title: 22.10.3 Key Performance Indicators

items: Target: Disciplinary incident rate below 5% of the student population each term
Calculation: (Students with Level 2+ incidents ÷ Total enrollment) × 100
Tracked monthly and reported termly

content.text: Restorative Agreement Completion:

items: Target: 80%+ successful completion of restorative agreements
Calculation: (Agreements fully completed ÷ Total agreements made) × 100
Tracked per agreement; reported termly

content.text: Repeat Offense Reduction:

items: Target: Reduce repeat offenses by 10% annually
Calculation: Compare students with multiple incidents from one year to the next
Reported annually

content.text: Student Wellbeing Survey:

items: Target: Student satisfaction with school climate above 85%
Questions cover feeling safe, feeling respected, and whether rules are fair
Administered annually; results inform improvement

content.text: Staff Confidence:

items: Target: 90%+ staff confident in managing behavior

content.text:
Staff receive training so they can carry out this policy well:

**Annual Policy Refresher:** All staff review the discipline policy and procedures on the professional development days at the start of the year. This includes updates, case studies, and Q&A.

**Restorative Practices Training:** Mandatory for all teachers. It covers the ideas behind restorative practice, affective statements, restorative questions, and classroom circles (6 hours). The SC Coordinator and Counselor receive advanced training on leading formal conferences (16+ hours). Annual refresher training.

**Classroom Management:** Part of the DTP (Development of Teaching Proficiency) program modules on managing learning environments. New teacher induction includes specific training on behavior expectations and procedures.

**Cultural Sensitivity:** Training on different cultural backgrounds, communication styles, and EAL (English as an Additional Language) needs in behavior management. Staff learn how cultural factors may affect both student behavior and the way adults respond.

**De-escalation Techniques:** Practical training to manage difficult situations safely: recognizing escalation, calming techniques, when to ask for help, and physical safety.

**Trauma-Informed Practice:** Awareness training on how trauma affects student behavior. It covers how to respond with support while keeping expectations.

**Peer Mediation Training:** The SC Coordinator and Counselor are trained to deliver the training program for student peer mediators.

**Cross-Reference:** See Section 12.6 for the DTP professional development framework.
This policy is reviewed every year: Timeline:
content.title: 22.13.1 Annual Review Process

items: April-May: Gather feedback from stakeholders
June: Analyze the behavior data for the year
July: Policy review committee meets
August: Revisions finalized and approved
September: The updated policy is shared and put into practice

editorialNotes.title: Source verification
editorialNotes.text: UU No. 12/2022 tentang Tindak Pidana Kekerasan Seksual (TPKS) is in force and governs sexual violence offenses. Permendikdasmen No. 6/2026 (BSAN) leans on it, together with UU No. 35/2014, for its sanctions provisions rather than carrying a self-contained ladder — this reliance matches the archived extraction of BSAN (docs/research/permendiknas/no-6-2026-bsan.json). [Source status, 2026-08-20: the TPKS characterization itself is not archive-backed — UU No. 12/2022 is not held in Desktop/Eduversal Sources/mevzuat/ and is not extracted into docs/research/. Verify against the UU TPKS salinan before treating it as verified. An earlier note here dated 2026-08-16 claimed verification against the source statute but pointed at a curriculum regulation PDF (Permendikbudristek 12-2024 - Kurikulum), the wrong document; that claim was withdrawn.]
